pages.summary: Cross-correlation and cross-covariance of signals, at every lag.
body: `xcorr` gives r(m), the sum of x(n+m) conj(y(n)), at lags -(N-1) to N-1 (or up to maxlag), the shorter signal padded with zeros; with one signal, its autocorrelation, and with a matrix every pair of columns. `'biased'` divides by N, `'unbiased'` by N - |m|, `'normalized'` makes the autocorrelation 1 at lag 0. `xcov` does the same with the signals' means taken off first. The lag of the largest value is the delay between two signals.

examples.title: An echo found

pages.summary: The delay between two signals, and the signals lined up.
body: `finddelay` gives the delay of y behind x in samples (negative when y is ahead): where their normalized cross-correlation is largest in absolute value, the smallest delay on a tie, column by column for matrices. `alignsignals` delays the earlier signal by leading zeros so that the two line up (`'truncate'` keeps it at its length), and gives the delay.
syntax: The delay of y behind x.

examples.title: A pulse that arrives late

body: `resample` changes the rate by p/q through a polyphase lowpass filter. `decimate` lowpass filters (a Chebyshev type I filter of order 8 run both ways, or `'fir'`) and keeps every r-th sample from the first; `interp` puts r - 1 samples between each pair by lowpass interpolation, keeping the signal's own. `downsample` and `upsample` only take samples out or put zeros in, without filtering, so that `downsample` lets higher frequencies fold back (alias).

examples.title: From 48 to 32 samples a cycle, and back
Aliasing, and none

pages.summary: A signal cut into frames, overlapping or with gaps.
body: Columns of n samples, each overlapping the one before by p (or skipping -p samples between them when p is negative); with p > 0 the first frame starts with p zeros. The last frame is padded with zeros, or with a second output, left out and given back as the samples that did not fill it.

pages.summary: Local maxima of a signal: their heights, places, widths and prominences.
body: A peak is higher than both its neighbours (a flat one counts where it starts; the ends never do). The options keep the peaks at least `'MinPeakHeight'` high, `'MinPeakProminence'` above the higher of the lowest points on either side before a higher peak, `'MinPeakDistance'` apart (the highest kept first), or `'Threshold'` above their neighbours; `'NPeaks'` and `'SortStr'` choose and order them. Widths are measured at half the prominence (or half the height), between linear crossings. With x or fs the places are in those units. Without outputs the signal is drawn with the peaks marked.

examples.title: The prominent peaks of a bumpy signal

pages.summary: The analytic signal, the envelope, and the instantaneous frequency.
body: `hilbert` gives x + i H(x), H the Hilbert transform (by the FFT, n points if given): its magnitude is the envelope and its angle the instantaneous phase. `envelope` gives upper and lower envelopes: from the analytic signal of x less its mean (the default), or (`'peak'`) splines through local maxima and minima at least np samples apart; without outputs it draws them. `instfreq` gives the instantaneous frequency: by default the mean frequency of each time slice of `pspectrum`'s spectrogram, or (`'Method', 'hilbert'`) the derivative of the analytic signal's phase at each sample.

examples.title: A modulated tone's envelope and frequency

pages.summary: Spectral windows: tapers that trade a wider main lobe for lower side lobes.
body: Each gives a column of n weights. Hamming and Hann are raised cosines (Hann reaching 0 at its ends; `hanning` leaves the zero ends off); Blackman, Blackman-Harris and Nuttall add more cosine terms for lower side lobes; the flat-top window measures amplitudes accurately; Kaiser's beta (0.5) trades lobe width for side lobes continuously. `'periodic'` makes a window for spectral analysis, one point longer and the last left off, so that it repeats.

examples.title: Shapes and side lobes

pages.summary: More windows, and windows by their functions.
body: Bartlett's triangle reaches 0 at its ends, `triang` does not; `rectwin` is ones; `gausswin` a Gaussian with alpha (2.5) the reciprocal of its standard deviation; `tukeywin` a tapered cosine, r (0.5) the part tapered (0 a rectangle, 1 a Hann window); `chebwin` has every side lobe r dB (100) down; the modified Bartlett-Hann, Bohman and Parzen windows are smooth tapers of their own. `window` calls a window's function with n and its other inputs.

examples.title: Triangles and tapers
examples.code:
[bartlett(5) triang(5)]
round(tukeywin(7, 0.5)', 3)
isequal(window(@gausswin, 7, 3), gausswin(7, 3))
plot([gausswin(64) tukeywin(64, 0.3) chebwin(64, 60) parzenwin(64)]), legend('gausswin', 'tukeywin 0.3', 'chebwin 60', 'parzenwin')

pages.summary: Power spectral densities, and the power in a band.
body: `periodogram` takes the squared magnitude of the whole signal's FFT (through a window if given, rectangular by default), at max(256, the next power of 2) frequencies, one-sided for real signals; `pwelch` averages the periodograms of windowed segments (8 Hamming segments half overlapping by default), smoother but coarser. Frequencies are in rad/sample, or in Hz with fs. Without outputs each is drawn in dB. `bandpower` gives the average power of a signal, or of the part in a band, from the signal or from a density.
syntax: [pxx, f] = pwelch(x, window, noverlap, nfft, fs)

examples.title: Two tones in noise

pages.summary: Two signals' cross spectrum, their coherence, and the transfer function from one to the other.
body: By Welch's method: `cpsd` gives the cross power spectral density; `mscohere` the magnitude-squared coherence, from 0 to 1 at each frequency (1 where y is a linear function of x); `tfestimate` the transfer function from x to y, their cross spectrum over the spectrum of x.
syntax: [pxy, f] = cpsd(x, y, window, noverlap, nfft, fs)
[cxy, f] = mscohere(x, y, window, noverlap, nfft, fs)
[txy, f] = tfestimate(x, y, window, noverlap, nfft, fs)

examples.title: A filter found from its input and output

pages.summary: Short-time Fourier transforms: spectra of windowed segments, and the signal back from them.
body: `spectrogram` gives a spectrum for each segment (8 Hamming segments half overlapping by default), the frequencies, the segments' middle times, and the power spectral density; without outputs it draws an image in dB. `stft` takes a periodic Hann window of 128 with 75% overlap unless given, the frequencies centred (from -fs/2 to fs/2) unless `'FrequencyRange'` says `'twosided'` or `'onesided'`; `istft` overlaps and adds the segments' inverse FFTs back into the signal, given the same options; a sample is back exactly when some segment's window is not 0 there, and the result is real for `'onesided'` transforms or with `'ConjugateSymmetric'`.
syntax: [s, f, t] = spectrogram(x, window, noverlap, nfft, fs)
[s, f, t] = stft(x, fs, 'Window', win, 'OverlapLength', n, 'FFTLength', nfft)
[x, t] = istft(s, fs, 'Window', win, 'OverlapLength', n, 'FFTLength', nfft)

examples.title: There and back
examples.intro: A window with no zeros, so that every sample is carried by some segment; the last samples, short of a whole segment, are left off.

pages.summary: The power spectrum, or a spectrogram, with sensible choices made.
body: A Kaiser window of beta 40(1 - Leakage) (Leakage 0.5) over the signal, scaled so that a sinusoid of amplitude A peaks at A²/2: the power of each tone can be read off. The `'power'` spectrum comes at at least 4096 frequencies from 0 to fs/2; the `'spectrogram'` in windows of about an eighth of the signal (or `'TimeResolution'` seconds), half overlapping unless `'OverlapPercent'` says. `'FrequencyLimits'` keeps a band, and `'MinThreshold'` sets values below it to 0. Without outputs it is drawn.

examples.title: Tones whose power can be read off

pages.summary: The Wigner-Ville distribution: time and frequency at once, as sharply as one signal allows.
body: At each time n, the FFT over lags m of z(n+m) conj(z(n-m)), z the analytic signal of x (x itself when complex). A single chirp shows as a sharp line; several components make cross terms between them, which `'smoothedPseudo'` smooths away in time and frequency (with Kaiser windows, or twin and fwin), at some cost in sharpness.
syntax: [d, f, t] = wvd(x, fs, 'smoothedPseudo', twin, fwin)
